Śabarotsava
(‘festival of the śabaras [aboriginals]’)
------------------------------------------
Śabarotsava is a part of the दुर्गा-पूजा celebrations. On the विजयदशमी or the tenth day (of Āśvayuja-śukla-पक्ष, bright half of Āśvayuja month, generally in October) the clay-image of मोथेर् दुर्गा has to be ceremonially immersed in the waters of a river or a lake. After the immersion, when the crowd of devotees is returning, it is expected to behave like the śabaras or aboriginal tribes. Some of the items of such uncivilised behaviour are: making merry to one’s heart’s content by throwing mud and dust, abusing one another using offensive words, singing erotic songs and so on.
All, irrespective of their status in the society, were expected to join in this revelry, probably emphasizing the equality before the मोथेर् of the universe.
See also DURGĀPŪJĀ.

Śabarīmalai
(‘the hill of शबरी’)
------------------------------------------
Śabarīmalai or Śabarigiri is one of the most popular places of पिल्ग्रिमगे even now. It is said to have got this name from शबरी, the humble lady-saint of the Rāmāyaṇa fame, who lived here and attained लिबेरतिओन्. It is 190 kms. (118 miles) to the north of Thiruvanantapuram (Trivandrum), the capital of the Kerala State. The hill is 950 metres (3100 feet) above the sea-level and 12 metres (40 feet) from the surrounding ground level. On its top is situated the temple of अय्यप्पन् (Ārya or शास्ता) (See ŚĀSTĀ for details regarding this deity.).
According to the local legends, the temple was built by Viśvakarman, the architect of the gods, and the original image of the deity prepared by the sage परशुराम. The present image which is 46 cms. (18 inches) in height is made of pañcaloha (five different metals) and installed after a devastating fire destroyed the temple in A.

.
One of the special features of the hill is the Patineṭṭupaḍi, a flight of eighteen steps. This is supposed to be the ladder to हेअवेन्.
These steps are about 1.8 metres (6 feet long and 20 cms. (8 inches) wide and very steep. They represent eighteen principles (5 sense organs, 8 internal enemies like lust and greed, 3 guṇas and विद्या as also अविद्या) which have to be transcended to reach God. They are to be climbed only by those devotees who have taken the prescribed vows.
The vow comprises the following disciplines and has to be strictly observed for 41 days before the darśan (seeing) of the image in the temple; wearing black, blue or ochre dress; wearing a रुद्राक्ष or तुलसी garland (of beads); strict celibacy during the period; visiting temples, avoiding meat, alcoholic drinks and drugs.
Initiation into this vow is to be done under the guidance of a गुरु, either in a temple or in one’s होउसे. It consists of preparing an Irumuḍi, a bag-like contrivance with two compartments. One compartment must contain a coconut filled with pure ghee (to be used to bathe the image) and some items necessary for worship. The other compartment should be filled with ड़ोओद् articles needed for the journey. This Irumuḍi has to be carried all the way on one’s own head.
The पिल्ग्रिमगे season is from November to March. From mid-November to mid-December, the temple is opened for 41 days. मकर सङ्क्रान्ति (usually on January 14) is the most crowded time of the year. It is on this day that Makaraviḷakku, a mysterious divine light, is seen on the Kāntamalai hill—also called Ponnambalameḍu—and disappears. Lakhs of devotees assemble on this day just to witness it.
The king Rājaśekhara had prepared a number of excellent ornaments for his adopted son मणिकण्ठन् or अय्यप्पन् to be worn on the day of his ascension to the throne. However, the young prince had refused to wear them, but had promised to be decorated by them on the मकर-सङ्क्रान्ति day every year. So, even now, these ornaments (called tiruvā-bharaṇam)—now in the possession of Rājaśekhara’s descendants—are brought from the palace of the king at Panthalam (88 kms. or 55 miles away from शबरी-malai) in a ceremonial procession and the image is richly bedecked with them just for a day.
Another aspect of this पिल्ग्रिमगे by the devotees to शबरीमलै is taking a bath in the river पम्पा. This small river takes its birth in the nearby Kāntamalai hill and flows below the 18 steps of the temple. It is said to have been brought to this earth from हेअवेन् by परमेश्वर (or शिव) himself.
Women in the menstruation age are not allowed to enter the temple since अय्यप्पन् is a strict celibate!
The total number of festivals observed in this temple is 16.

śabdapramāṇa
------------------------------------------
Śabdapramāṇa is the same as शब्द or verbal testimony.
See MĪMĀṀSĀDARŚANA.

śabda
(‘sound’)
------------------------------------------
Śabda is a term of several connotations. In its simplest form it means sound in general.
In Vedānta philosophy it means शब्द-tanmātra, the element आकाश (space or ether) in its purest form. It also, sometimes, indicates the Śruti or the Veda.
In grammar it denotes a word made up of letters and conveying some meaning. It is then described as sārthaka or with meaning. Words or letters without any particular meaning are called nirarthaka. It is also classed into three groups according to gender: pulliṅga (masculine gender), strīliṅga (feminine gender) and napuṁsakaliṅga (neuter gender).
The पूर्वमीमाṁसा philosophy categorises the Vedic words into five classes as: विधि (injunction), मन्त्र (sacred utterance), nāmadheya (nomenclature), निषेध (prohibition) and अर्थवाद (eulogy).
It also recognises that śabdas or words can be laukika (pertaining to mundane affairs), which again can be classified as विधि, निषेध and अर्थवाद.
Śabdas or words of reliable persons (āptavākya) as also Vedic words are considered pramāṇa (valid source of knowledge).
The Amarakośa (7) gives different names to different kinds of sounds such as marmara (sound of leaves), śiñjita (sound of ornaments when one is moving), kvaṇana (sweet sound of musical instruments), ruta (sound of certain animals and birds), gāna (music) and so on.

According to him, ब्रह्मन् (who is advaita or one without a second) is चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and that चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is the power of speech, which again is of the nature of शब्द, sound or vibration. Hence ब्रह्मन् is of the nature of ‘śabda’ or speech.
Though Maṇḍana, following Bhartṛ-hari (5th century A. D.), a philosopher of the school of grammar, adduces several powerful arguments in its favour, later advaitins do not subscribe to his views.

Śabdabrahman
(‘Brahman in the form of शब्द or sound’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in several senses.
The Veda is known as ब्रह्मन् since it helps us in realising ब्रह्मन् or God, the Absolute. It is also in the form of शब्द or words. Hence it is called शब्दब्रह्मन्.
The word Oṁ (Praṇava) is the highest symbol of ब्रह्मन्. The उपनिषद्स् identify it with ब्रह्मन् (vide Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8.1; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.15). Hence शब्दब्रह्मन् is ओङ्कार.
The Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad (17) identifies Saguṇabrahman (Brahman with attributes) with शब्दब्रह्मन् and Nirguṇabrahman (Brahman without attri-butes) with परब्रह्मन्.
This word occurs in the Bhagavadgītā (6.44) also. It has been interpreted there as the result of Vedic rituals (Śaṅkara) or the प्रकृति or nature (Rāmānuja).

Śābara-bhāṣya
(‘commentary by Śabara-svāmin’)
------------------------------------------
The basic work of the Mimāṁsā philosophy—one of the six systems of Hindu philosophy—is the Pūrvamīmāṁsā Sūtras of जैमिनि assigned to 200 B. C. The earliest extant commentary on it is the Śābarabhāṣya (or Śabarabhāṣya) attributed to Śabarasvāmi who might have lived either during 57 B. C. or during A.

.
According to some scholars he was the ड़थेर् of the king विक्रमादित्य (of the Vikrama Era fame), by his क्षत्त्रिय wife.
The commentary, in chaste (and ideal) Sanskrit prose, is quite voluminous, dealing with all aspects of interpretation of the वेदस्.
